item.title: My 102nd Parkrun, 51F and VO2max Back to 50
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

My 102nd parkrun today: 51F with a bit drizzle. Nothing to write home about, but I did get a minute faster than last time, and avg pace is 8’09”/mi approaching sub-8’. Still a long way to go from my PR 21:05, but hey one small step a time!

And with that, my VO2max is back to 50!

Originally posted on Mastodon.

item.title: Mira Murati on Interaction Models and Keeping Humans in the Loop
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

At Bloomberg Tech 2026 in San Francisco, Bloomberg’s Emily Chang interviewed Mira Murati, co-founder and CEO of Thinking Machines Lab, the AI lab she started in February 2025 after leaving OpenAI, where she had been CTO. The 28-minute conversation covers the lab’s first public bet (interaction models), her account of the November 2023 OpenAI board crisis, the war for AI talent, and why she’s building toward human-AI collaboration rather than the autonomy-first path most labs are racing down.

With the help of AI, I’ve built an enriched transcript at the bottom of this post — the video’s auto-captions, reorganized into chapters with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor’s-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for details.

A few takeaways worth jumping to:

  • Interaction models are an interface bet: continuous, time-based models that take in audio, text, and video in 20-millisecond chunks, rather than the turn-based prompt-then-wait loop of today’s models.
  • She bets on collaboration over autonomy: she grants the autonomy-first path is the faster way to advance AI, and chooses instead to bring machine intelligence closer to human intent.
  • She casts November 2023 as a governance failure: her one regret is not pausing on the transition plan; she leaves the question of whether removing Altman was right unanswered.
  • “Humans in the loop” as a tandem bike: both riders pedaling, both hands on the wheel, with alignment offered as a byproduct of collaboration.

  • 0:02:45 — The bet: human-AI collaboration over pure autonomy (YouTube)
  • 0:05:26 — AI as a tool for thought (YouTube)

  • 0:20:28 — Jobs, dystopia, and agency (YouTube)
  • 0:22:15 — Will humans always be in the loop? (YouTube)
  • 0:23:40 — Killer instinct and competition (YouTube)
  • 0:25:44 — The preview, and resisting short-term pressure (YouTube)
  • 0:27:16 — Success beyond wildest expectations (YouTube)

My Notes

  • New tools can change how we think. Positional notation didn’t just speed up arithmetic over Roman numerals, it changed what mathematics a person could attempt, and the idea that representational systems shape cognition runs from writing to Kenneth Iverson’s “notation as a tool of thought”. What she raises but doesn’t answer is whether AI tools are a notation-level shift that expands what we can think about, or an accelerant that speeds up the thinking we already do.

  • Institutional design over individual virtue. “Morality is not everything,” she says, pointing instead to decision-making structures, transparency, and governance, because “even people who are well-intentioned can make mistakes.” Good individual intentions don’t guarantee good outcomes at the organizational level, where morality is an emergent property of incentives and structure and can degrade even when everyone inside means well. That gap between personal ethics and what an institution produces is the failure mode Robert Jackall’s Moral Mazes [1] documents. It’s notable coming from a frontier-lab CEO, since the AI-governance conversation mostly fixates on founder character (“whose hand is on the dial”), which she’s arguing is the less durable lever.

  • Her focus on human agency lines up with the Pope’s. The tandem-bike image puts the person at the center of the design rather than efficiency. That is close to Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical on AI, which makes the dignity of the human person the measure for AI ahead of efficiency or profit.

  • “Human-in-the-loop leads to alignment” needs to be validated. She says collaboration gets you value-alignment “as a result of this approach.” Learning from humans in the loop isn’t new: RLHF is exactly that. But RLHF aligns a model to human intent, following instructions and preferences, which isn’t the same as aligning it to human values: a model can do what you asked and still optimize for something you don’t endorse. The signal differs in kind, and whether training to follow the former can lead to adherence to the latter needs further investigation.

  • Is humans-in-the-loop just a waypoint? She defends keeping humans in the loop in time-bound terms: “for as long as we can,” and making sure “this period” is meaningful. Asked directly whether humans might eventually leave the loop, she answers “it is possible.” So the position may be less “humans belong in the loop” than “removing them now would forfeit our chance to get the transition right.” That leaves open whether the destination is still full autonomy, approached more carefully. It’s the same question that runs through the automation-vs-augmentation debate.

Transcript

What’s here is the auto-generated transcript from the YouTube video, reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The dialog is verbatim in substance but lightly edited for readability — filler words and stutters removed, punctuation, capitalization, and paragraph breaks added (auto-captions ship without them). Nothing was paraphrased or reordered. Four editorial layers have been added:

  • Chapter outline. 14 chapters, each linking to its YouTube timestamp. The titles are editorial summaries of what’s being discussed, not verbatim quotes. The full outline is in the right-hand sidebar.
  • Inline hyperlinks. First mention of a salient person, company, or concept links to an authoritative source.
  • Bracketed expansions. Where an acronym appears without being spelled out in speech, the expansion is inserted in [square brackets] to mark it as editorial.
  • Editor’s notes in blue callout boxes flag dates and figures worth checking.

Speaker attribution was reconstructed from the captions’ speaker-change markers, so a stray line may be mislabeled. Obvious mishearings of names were corrected silently — ChatGPT, OpenAI, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, GPT-4o, o1 — and one content word was an inferred fix (nuances for the captions’ “neurons”).

0:00:00 — What interaction models are: continuous, not turn-based

Emily Chang: Let’s start with today and what you’re working on. You are building interaction models at Thinking Machines — models that you say keep humans in the loop. What exactly does that mean?

Mira Murati: We’ve been working for the past year and a half on the foundations of building a frontier AI lab, with the specific focus that we have. And the interaction models were a first look at our concentrated bet toward human-AI collaboration.

The reason why we even started Thinking Machines is because we wanted to build the frontier AI lab that’s really focused on the human-AI collaboration piece. That means a lot of things, and there are specific research bets that go into that, but we wanted to showcase our work in one of the first bets through the interaction models.

The interaction models are a new kind of model. If you consider the types of models that we work with today, they’re very turn-based. And so you talk, they talk, then they go off and think.

Once you’ve given a prompt on what it is that you want to do, while they’re thinking, it’s almost like they’re deaf and blind. They cannot perceive anything else about what’s going on. And then it’s your turn. And while you’re talking, they really cannot perceive anything about how you’re talking. It’s not happening in real time.

By contrast, our interactions with each other are very rich. There is a lot of information in our interactions — when we are silent, when we’re thinking, when we’re interrupting one another. And so interaction models are able to capture all of these nuances.

They’re not turn-based, they’re more like time-based interaction, where they’re continuously taking in audio, text, and video and continuously providing output. Now, we cut this up in chunks of 20 milliseconds.

And this enables you to actually catch these things like interruptions and simultaneous speech, and really create a rich, high-bandwidth interaction between humans and machines, which we think is critical to enable agency and to enable people to be more in this loop as we advance AI further and further.

0:02:45 — The bet: human-AI collaboration over pure autonomy

Emily Chang: You’re basically trying to build an AGI [artificial general intelligence] lab from scratch. You’ve got OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, all with a significant head start, all of them racing to build smarter models. What is the bet that you’re making that they aren’t, and what do you think they are underestimating?

Mira Murati: So first of all, I think advancing the frontier of AI is incredibly positive-sum, and there is plenty of space for many different perspectives and ways of developing the technology. I think plurality is good — having a plurality of perspectives, of ways of building technology, different products, is great for the world.

Now, this is a pretty hard thing to do, so I think that’s why we don’t actually have many players. The barrier to entry is incredibly high. But in terms of creating something differentiated, I do think there is plenty of room.

I have always been very passionate about advancing the frontier of AI systems, and I think there is a potential for so much transformation for civilization that comes from that. But it’s not a predestined outcome. The way that we go about building it and deploying the systems really matters. And an area where there is very little work that’s been done so far is bringing the machine intelligence closer to where the knowledge is.

What I mean by that is, there is one path of advancing frontier systems which is very autonomous and doesn’t rely too much on the messiness of reality, or the experience that humans have day-to-day — and that’s quite a fast way of advancing AI systems, very autonomously. Autonomy is definitely a part of it, and it’s a very important part. But a missing part, where we haven’t done much work, is really focusing on human intent, on the messiness of interaction, enabling people more, and conceptually building frontier systems more like tools for thought. I think the most advanced AI systems are the most incredible tools for thought that humanity can ever have.

0:05:26 — AI as a tool for thought

Emily Chang: And so how can this change the way that we think?

Mira Murati: We’re still thinking — but it’s changing the nature of thought, what we’re thinking about. And this part is familiar to us. Since the beginning of time, deep technologies have changed what we think about: language, writing, numerals. Imagine if you had to do multiplication with Roman numerals — it would be miserable. But we invented today’s numerals, and this enabled a whole area of mathematics. A child can do mathematics very quickly. So it enabled these very tangible new ways of thought. And I think this is the opportunity ahead of us — this possibility to expand what we think about, and have new tangible things that we think about. And this requires very intentional research work and product work in this direction.

0:06:42 — Leaving OpenAI: running toward something

Emily Chang: When I interviewed you, it was early 2023. ChatGPT had just changed everything, and you were CTO of OpenAI. A few folks I talked to said you basically ran the place — just saying. When you left to found Thinking Machines, were you running toward something or away from something?

Mira Murati: I most definitely was running toward something, once I figured out what that was. But I had an incredible experience at OpenAI. I was so incredibly lucky to work with some of the most dedicated and most talented people in the world, and that’s incredibly special. I’m very grateful for that experience.

Eventually I had my own view — a very strong view — of how I think this technology ought to be developed, and it’s very rare to start something from scratch once you have developed such a strong perspective on it. That’s a rare privilege to have. I think having a company like Thinking Machines gives us an opportunity to focus on where we have the highest conviction, and build and orient the entire company around that conviction.

0:08:17 — The board crisis, in retrospect

Emily Chang: Take me back to the board crisis of that year. Later that year, you testified under oath that you were worried OpenAI was at catastrophic risk of falling apart. You raised concerns about Sam Altman’s leadership. But in that moment, you had to act. Looking back, do you think you got that right?

Mira Murati: It was a very intense time, and a very complex situation. I’m sure many people have been in situations that felt impossible, where you have to make really hard calls very quickly.

There is a part of this complexity that wasn’t visible to the world — it appeared that it happened overnight, but to me it was years of thinking about the mission, the governance, how you build a team that can build durable, transformational technologies with that responsibility. There was a lot of complexity to the organization that had been there for years, and that we had thought about a lot.

This particular thing that happened, this acute moment — there was a lot of intensity to it, and very little time. When the board asked me for feedback, I shared feedback, and I stand by that. When they made the decision and asked me to step up as interim CEO, I did that. And when I realized that their decision was potentially catastrophic for the company and things would potentially fall apart, I felt like I had to act very quickly.

Even though on the surface it just looked very chaotic, at each point in time I felt very clear about what I had to do — because the thing that I cared the most about was the mission, the continuity of the mission, and the people and the team. This is not an abstract thing. It’s real people that I worked with for many years and cared very deeply about, and all of this was about to potentially implode.

So it was very clear to me what I had to do — to provide continuity, stability, and help bring Sam back, restore that, get the team in place to then deliver GPT-4o and o1. It was that principle that made it very clear to me what I had to do.

In retrospect, I think that I would have paused more on understanding the transition plan. With the benefit of hindsight, there wasn’t any transition plan, and there wasn’t much thought put into transparency — bringing the team along, providing continuity. In retrospect, I would have paused more on that.

Note

Editor’s note. The sequence: OpenAI’s board removed Sam Altman on November 17, 2023; Murati was named interim CEO; Altman was reinstated about five days later, and Murati returned to her role as CTO. Her “testified under oath” refers to deposition testimony in the litigation between Elon Musk and OpenAI. The two models she cites as what the team went on to deliver, GPT-4o and o1, were released in May and September 2024 respectively. Murati was OpenAI’s CTO from May 2022 until she left in September 2024.

Emily Chang: Interesting. Helen Toner, a former OpenAI board member, said: “Mira was waiting to see which way the wind would blow, and she didn’t realize she was the wind.” What do you think would have happened if you didn’t do what you did?

Mira Murati: I think quite likely OpenAI would have…

0:11:51 — Whose hand is on the dial: character vs. governance

Emily Chang: The case got thrown out on a technicality, so the court never decided whether the leaders of OpenAI breached their mission. How much does the character of the people building the most powerful technology in the world matter? Whose hand is on the dial?

Mira Murati: I think the integrity, character, and values of the people matter a lot, because there are a lot of decisions — micro-decisions — you have to make every day, and you have to trust your team that they’re making the right calls. There’s plenty of focus on that, and that’s great. Where there is less focus is the institutional design, decision-making, transparency — increasing the level of agency that people have to actually decide for themselves. So it doesn’t have to be an authority that says “this is safe, this is good, stamp of approval” — each person can weigh for themselves what works for them.

I think the way that we’re going about building AI systems today is very concentrated, and it’s partly the legacy way, because we didn’t have real-world data and experience. The only way to advance AI was in a silo, in a vacuum. But today is a different time to build, where we can actually learn a lot from the capabilities, tensions, and limitations in the real world, and use that data and information to steer the direction of research. This enables people to think for themselves.

Often people will ask me about ChatGPT and the impact of all of that. Of course it’s magnificent from a technology perspective, but I think the most important impact of ChatGPT in the public consciousness is that everyone kind of understands what it is by interacting with it, versus being told what AI can do and what its capabilities and limitations are.

0:14:14 — What the moment demands of a leader

Emily Chang: What do you think this moment demands of a leader, and should we trust the leaders in power right now?

Mira Murati: I think everyone should have the tools and information to make these decisions for themselves. Ideally, the structure of governance and decision-making should not hinge on one person. There should be checks and balances. I think it’s very important who is working on the systems, and the character of people. But I do think the conversation gets too wrapped up there, and not enough on thinking more broadly about checks and balances in the system — because even people who are well-intentioned can make mistakes, and they can misestimate the consequences of making a call.

So morality is not everything. You have to think about actual decision-making structures, and transparency, and governance. These are all complicated things. And to get as many people involved as possible, you actually have to share the knowledge. You have to share tools. This is part of the reason why we’ve taken a more open approach with our lab.

0:15:48 — Building Thinking Machines: the tandem bike

Emily Chang: So that was my next question — how is everything that you’ve learned shaping what you’re building at Thinking Machines, and how you’re building it, and the culture that you want to create?

Mira Murati: I have very high conviction that the way to continue building frontier AI systems is to bring people along, and to have humans in the loop. Actually, “having humans in the loop” doesn’t quite describe it, because it sounds like a checkpoint where we’re signing off on something and then you’re good to go.

It’s more like creating systems that are not just autonomously advancing and leaving civilization behind, but are more like a tandem bike where both people are pedaling. When you’re going up a hill, maybe whoever is stronger is pedaling harder, but both hands are on the wheel.

And that’s quite important, because that’s a different system — a system designed for collaboration. That’s what we’re trying to build with Thinking Machines.

I think it’s quite differentiated, and I hope that it will increase the level of agency that people have, and also help us steer the research direction toward creating outputs that are more value-aligned. So you also get alignment as a result of this approach, in addition to usefulness — actually creating technologies that are useful in the real world.

0:17:39 — The war for talent

Emily Chang: You’ve hired a lot of top talent. We’ve seen reports of nine-figure deals. There have also been some high-profile departures. How would you describe the war for talent? How brutal is it?

Mira Murati: It’s definitely a big part of building a frontier AI lab — having the right people, people who have the competence to do it but are also aligned with your overall mission, conviction, what you’re trying to achieve. I wouldn’t call it a war, because that might mean that the highest bidder wins. For the most part, people working in this field genuinely care about advancing the field. Now, it is an absolutely crazy time, and a lot of it is unprecedented. It’s incredibly intense to build a frontier AI lab from scratch during such competitive times. That leads to a lot of uncertainty, unpredictability, some of the volatility that we’ve seen. But when you’re trying to compress progress into such a short amount of time, things that happen in other startups over the course of ten years, five years — both good and bad — are going to happen in the course of a few months, or a year. Part of what we’re seeing is contextualized in that: just compressing the amount of progress that’s happening. And whenever you have something good, something bad will come with it, so you have to balance the two.

People leave for different reasons — maybe their passion evolves for what they want to work on. The high compensation numbers capture the imagination of people because obviously they’re very big, but I do think that for some of the most sought-after people, that’s not the main story.

There is a lot that goes on here, and it is very intense to build a company from scratch, let alone a frontier AI lab. So that’s part of the challenges and suffering of building a company and doing anything zero to one.

0:20:28 — Jobs, dystopia, and agency

Emily Chang: Dario Amodei has predicted mass white-collar job loss. Sam, though, recently walked back some of his predictions about a jobs apocalypse. Where do you think the industry is being too pessimistic, and too optimistic? What is Mira Murati’s vision for the future?

Mira Murati: Predicting a dystopia or a utopia, to me, feels very simplified, because the truth is we actually have a lot of agency in how we build this technology — in the tools that we’re building, in how we’re deploying it. It’s not a predestined outcome.

There are certainly risks; we all understand the potential for greatness that comes with building frontier AI systems, and that’s why we’re working on them. There’s been a lot of talk around the uncertainty and the downsides, and I agree with a lot of these risks. Perhaps where I might disagree, or take a different path, is that I think we have a lot of agency.

This period of time, where both humans and AI systems have their hands on the wheel and we can collaborate, is a very important time to get right. And the more that we can reduce the discontinuity that comes from new capabilities and huge changes in capabilities, the better. This is why we took this approach with Thinking Machines, and why the company exists.

Note

Editor’s note. Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, warned in May 2025 that AI could eliminate up to half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years and push unemployment to 10–20%. The “Sam” who walked back jobs-apocalypse predictions is Sam Altman of OpenAI.

0:22:15 — Will humans always be in the loop?

Emily Chang: So you say the goal is to keep humans in the loop. But is there ever a point where humans don’t need to be in the loop — and then what happens?

Mira Murati: It is possible. It’s more about aligning at that point — aligning intent and aligning values. But if you reduce progress to removing humans from this loop of development already now, then I see very little future possibility that we can get this right when AI systems are even more capable.

So I think the more likely path, and the more durable path, to advance AI in a way that enables and advances civilization, is by keeping humans in the loop for as long as we can, and really making sure that this period is actually very meaningful.

0:23:40 — Killer instinct and competition

Emily Chang: You’ve raised a lot of money. There are great expectations. If anything’s clear from the last few months in AI news, it’s that there’s some cutthroat competition out there. Do you think you have that killer instinct to take on OpenAI and Anthropic and Meta and Google and China and X — it’s a competitive world.

Mira Murati: It is extremely competitive. And yeah, we did raise a lot of money. We’re proud of that, but that’s not any big accomplishment — we didn’t set out to break some sort of record. It’s really what you do with that.

We’re not a normal company, and so you do need a lot of capital in order to build the infrastructure, the foundations of science, and all that’s required to actually have a claim at building frontier AI systems that are differentiated. So that part in itself is not unique.

In terms of killer instinct — that’s not really what motivates me. I think there’s actually a lot of room. We’re building a technology that has infinite potential, and it’s going to be hard to capture all of that potential. What motivates me is really capturing part of that potential — creating useful things in the world, bringing the technology into the world in a way that’s useful and increases human agency and advances our civilization.

There is healthy competition, and competition is good — it creates better products and better technologies for people. It raises the bar in many ways. I respect a lot of the companies that are doing this. But my motivation, day to day, when I wake up in the morning — I am not thinking about how…

Note

Editor’s note. Thinking Machines Lab raised about $2 billion in a seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz at a reported $12 billion valuation (July 2025), with investors including Nvidia, AMD, Cisco, and Jane Street — one of the largest seed rounds on record.

0:25:44 — The preview, and resisting short-term pressure

Emily Chang: You’ve said you plan to release a preview later this year. How far along are you? And with all of these other companies going public, do you think they’ll be distracted and you’ll have a little more room to run?

Mira Murati: We’re on our own path. Of course, the competition is fierce and we have to move quickly, but it’s important to balance that with durable, long-term progress. I care a lot about the decisions that we make today being good for our long-term success, and that’s something that I really try to instill in the team day to day. There is a lot of detail here with how you build the team, how you build the infrastructure, and really resisting the short-term pressures. In some cases you do have to embrace the pressure. But for us, this is just a first step — showcasing the interaction models and making it more concrete what it is that we think about and care about. I expect the next few months to show increased capabilities on the model side, more products in this direction, and to make it more obvious — really letting the technology and the products speak for themselves.

0:27:16 — Success beyond wildest expectations

Emily Chang: So a Thinking Machine succeeds beyond your wildest expectations. What exists then?

Mira Murati: It is extremely difficult to predict the future. But I’d say the most important thing would be to create a future where, regardless of how many hours of work we do day to day or week to week, we feel a sense of agency, a sense of dignity, and possibility about the future. I hope we’ll continue to advance the capabilities that will enable a lot of progress, and that we’ll do it in a way that will keep us hopeful and with a sense of possibility that we can drive about the future.

Emily Chang: Well, here’s to less impossibility, and…

item.title: AI, Journalism, and the Uncertain Future of the Public Square
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

A. G. Sulzberger, publisher of the New York Times, used the opening remarks at the WAN-IFRA World News Media Congress in Marseille to make the news industry’s bluntest case yet against the companies leading the AI build-out. The Reuters Institute republished the full text. The speech was titled “AI, journalism and the uncertain future of the public square,” and its thesis is that the profession has been “too quiet, too passive and too fragmented” in the face of AI companies that take journalism without consent or compensation.

The speech’s central comparison puts “data” alongside AI’s other inputs:

The first is talent – the people who design the algorithms. The second is what tech companies call “compute.” […] The third is energy […] The fourth is what tech companies call “data.” The word itself seems almost designed to make creative and expressive work sound trivial, a ubiquitous commodity. But “data” is often used, among other things, as a synonym for books, movies, music and journalism – what might more accurately be called “copyrighted content.”

What the speech argues:

  • The asymmetry of inputs. Talent, compute, and energy are all paid for. No lab would ask its best engineers to work free or tap a power line illegally, but “data” is taken without consent or payment, justified by shifting rationales (it’s just facts, deals are slow, fair use covers it, national security demands it).
  • The scale gap. The six leading AI companies are worth a combined $11 trillion and US private AI investment hit ~$350 billion in 2025, yet by the speech’s estimate less than half of 1% of that goes to compensate the creators of the training data.
  • The traffic mechanism. Getting a Google user to click through is reportedly ten times harder than a decade ago. Competing AI products send referral traffic at a rate 96% lower than Google search. Comscore-tracked newspapers saw average traffic drops above 45% as the AI race intensified, and newspaper advertising revenue is already down 80% over two decades.
  • The reliability problem. A European Broadcasting Union study found leading AI assistants misrepresented the news in nearly half of all answers, and because models express uncertainty poorly they tend to be “confidently wrong,” while disclaiming legal responsibility for what they output.
  • Four ways to fight back.
    • Stand up for your rights: insist that intellectual-property (IP) rights be respected, and push back when they aren’t.
    • Deal carefully: weigh each licensing deal’s long-term value before signing.
    • Push legislators: reinforce IP protections, require bots to identify themselves, mandate usage transparency, and make AI companies liable for defamatory output.
    • Join together: coordinate across the industry and with other creative sectors.
  • Four ways to stay resilient.
    • Use AI the right way: set newsroom standards, then put the technology to work.
    • Be a destination: build direct audience relationships instead of relying on intermediated traffic.
    • Focus on original reporting: the work AI can’t do and has no other source for.
    • Explain why journalism matters: make the public case that original reporting is essential.

The speech is specific about who: Meta training on pirated books, Perplexity scraping against explicit objection, OpenAI lobbying for legal immunity, and even Anthropic, “often held up for its commitment to ethical AI development,” declining to pay for the journalism it uses. The Times is itself suing OpenAI and Microsoft, and later Perplexity, over these practices.

My Notes

  • The regurgitation charge has outside support: his strongest legal claim is “substitutive copying, retention and regurgitation” of individual works, and it is testable. A preprint covered in Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Reactivates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books found frontier models reproduce copyrighted books word-for-word, and that finetuning reactivates recall traced to pretraining.

  • The cure leans on advice already tried: “Be a destination” and “direct relationships with audiences” is the go-direct advice of the search/social era, and more than 3,000 US papers closed anyway. If AI intermediation is structural, and a 96% lower referral rate suggests it is, that advice may prove too little too late.

Related Posts

  • Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Reactivates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books: empirical support for Sulzberger’s “regurgitation” charge, showing frontier models reproduce copyrighted books word-for-word.
  • LLMs, Copyrighted Training Data, and Fair Use: the fair-use defense Sulzberger says AI labs lean on to take “data” without payment, examined on its legal merits.
  • AI-Generated Art Cannot Be Copyrighted, Rules a US Federal Judge: the output side of the same copyright fight, on whether AI generations are themselves protectable.
  • US Copyright Office Guidance on Generative AI: the regulatory backdrop to the IP-rights enforcement Sulzberger urges publishers to demand.

item.title: Greg Brockman on the Founding of OpenAI and the 72 Hours That Nearly Ended It
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In a Knowledge Project interview with Shane Parrish, OpenAI cofounder and president Greg Brockman walks through the company’s first decade: the 2015 dinner with Sam Altman, the Napa offsite that fixed OpenAI’s technical plan, the 72 hours in November 2023 when Altman was fired and the company nearly came apart, and where he thinks compute, jobs, and AGI (artificial general intelligence) go next. The conversation runs about 72 minutes.

The episode’s official written transcript is paywalled, but the full conversation is on YouTube, so I’ve built an enriched transcript at the bottom of this post: the YouTube auto-captions cleaned up and diarized, sliced into the video’s 34 chapters (each linking to its timestamp), with hyperlinks on first mention of every person, company, model, and concept, bracketed acronym expansions, and editor’s notes flagging claims worth a second look. The chapter outline is in the right-hand sidebar.

The conversation, in brief:

  • Meeting Sam Altman: how a 2015 dinner and a late-night drive turned into the decision to start OpenAI, against a consensus that DeepMind’s lead was insurmountable.
  • The founding plan still holds: the three-step bet sketched at the Napa offsite (solve reinforcement learning, then unsupervised learning, then progressively harder tasks) is the one OpenAI has run for a decade.
  • Why the nonprofit had to change: once they ran the compute math in 2017, nonprofit fundraising had a ceiling, and a for-profit arm became the only path to an AGI-scale budget.
  • The breakthroughs that felt real: the 2017 sentiment-neuron result and then Dota 2 convinced him that simple algorithms plus massive compute could reach human-level play in messy environments.
  • Prediction as a route to intelligence: Greg argues pretraining and reasoning run on the same machinery, predicting the next token on differently structured data.
  • The firing, hour by hour: where he was when the board called, the message he got, and why he quit that night.
  • He still won’t say why: Greg narrates the 72 hours in close detail but never names what actually drove the board’s decision.
  • The petition that crashed Google Docs: nearly the whole company signed, and Ilya’s overnight reversal was the moment he felt it could be put back together.
  • What he took from it: be decisive, have the hard conversation, and, in Ilya’s framing, accept that building something real means suffering.
  • AI building AI: code is “essentially all AI now,” with humans still ahead on structure and interfaces, and models starting to propose their own research ideas.
  • On sycophancy: models did start telling users what they wanted to hear, so OpenAI retrained against “hacking the grader” toward users’ long-term goals.
  • Why the reasoning traces went dark: distillation defense, plus keeping the chain-of-thought faithful instead of trained to look good.
  • A compute-constrained world: a personal AGI for everyone would need on the order of billions of GPUs, far past what’s being built, so who gets served becomes a real question.
  • The data-center bet: the spending OpenAI was teased for is, in his telling, what delivers the mission, and he entertains data centers in space.
  • The global race and regulation: why he thinks US leadership in AI matters, and where he would put guardrails (compute access, privacy and privilege, data-center water and power).
  • Jobs and what you gain: some institutions and roles won’t be as stable, but he frames the upside as agency, down to “a doctor in their pocket” for everyone.
  • Success: “ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity.”

Transcript

What’s here is the YouTube auto-caption transcript of the interview, reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The dialog is lightly edited for clarity (repeated words, stutters, and obvious false starts trimmed), not paraphrased or reordered, with several editorial layers added:

  • Chapter outline. The transcript is split into the video’s 34 YouTube chapters, each linking to its timestamp. The full outline is in the right-hand sidebar; use it to jump to a specific moment instead of scrolling.
  • Inline hyperlinks. First mention of every salient person, company, model, product, or concept links to an authoritative source. Research papers are cited by number and collected in the References at the end.
  • Bracketed acronym expansions. Where an acronym appears for the first time without being expanded in speech, the expansion is inserted in [square brackets] to mark it as editorial (e.g. AGI [artificial general intelligence]).
  • Editor’s notes in blue callout boxes flag claims that are verifiable and slightly off, statements worth dating against the public record, or numbers given without a source.

Two caveats specific to a YouTube source. Punctuation, capitalization, and paragraph breaks are editorial (auto-captions ship without them), and speaker attribution was reconstructed from YouTube’s speaker-change markers, so a stray line in the fast exchanges may be mislabeled. Obvious mishearings of proper nouns have been corrected silently: OpenAI (for “open AI”), Chris Olah, Jakub, Szymon, Aleksander (the colleagues who resigned alongside Brockman), Ilya, and Dota. Repeated words and phrase stutters have been collapsed and obvious false starts trimmed (I I → I, that was that was → that was), and three sponsor ad-reads (CoinShares, Granola, HeyGen and Element) have been removed as they are not part of the interview.

0:00:00 — Introduction

Shane Parrish: So, how did OpenAI come about?

Greg Brockman: Well, I knew I wanted to do a startup because I felt like that was something

Shane Parrish: But you were just in a startup. Stripe was a startup.

Greg Brockman: It’s true, but I felt like Stripe, the problem that we were solving was not my problem, right? It wasn’t the problem I’d grown up thinking about. It was an important problem and I dedicated myself to that mission for a number of years, but I felt like it was going to succeed with or without me.

And so, then I had a first moment to really think about what is a mission that I want to dedicate myself to where I would spend the rest of my life working on this problem just to see it play out in a slightly better way.

And it was very clear to me that top of the list was AI. Right?

0:00:49 — Meeting Sam Altman and Starting OpenAI

Greg Brockman: If you could actually make a difference in how AI will play out in the world like that would be a life well lived.

Shane Parrish: When you were thinking about leaving, Patrick told you to go talk to Sam Altman. What happened in that conversation?

Greg Brockman: Well, Patrick had said Sam has seen lots of young people in your situation and Patrick, I think, really hoped that Sam would convince me to stay. A few minutes of talking to Sam, he’s like, “Okay, you clearly have already decided. It is very obvious.”

And so, he asked, “Well, what are you planning on doing next?” And I said, “Well, I’m thinking about doing an AI company.” And he said, “I’m also thinking about doing something in AI. We should keep in touch.”

So, I had talked to Sam maybe one more time after I was leaving Stripe. And he asked, “Are you still thinking about doing something in AI?” I said, “Yes.” He said, “I’m also starting to get more details and putting together this dinner in July and I flew out for the dinner.

And the thing that I remember was a topic was, “Is it too late to start a lab with many of the best researchers? Is it possible?”

Shane Parrish: And this is what year?

Greg Brockman: 2015. Right? Because you think about just the degree to which DeepMind had all the researchers, all the capital, all the data, it just felt like is it even possible to get something off the ground still? People came up with all sorts of reasons it was hard. No one could come up with a reason it was actually impossible.

And so, Sam and I driving back to the city that night, I remember we looked at each other and we said, we got to do this. Right? Like we just have to. And so, next day I was full-time on putting this together.

And it was tough because it was very ill-defined. We had mission, a vision of saying, we think that we can build human level AI, make it be something positive for the world, make the benefits be something that are distributed broadly. But how?

0:02:40 — Building the Founding Team

Greg Brockman: And how do you get people to actually leave their jobs to come and join this thing? Initially, the set of people that I narrowed down to were actually Ilya Sutskever, Dario Amodei, Chris Olah, and myself. That was going to be the team. And we spent a lot of time together, we spent a lot of time talking about potential visions for the lab, potential ways that things would work. It didn’t quite come together, and that there was just partly a question of will this have enough momentum? You know, Dario felt like that he needed to go and establish a name for himself, and he wasn’t sure if this was really going to be it. It’s a question of just how it was all going to work.

And meanwhile, I was starting to get John Schulman interested. He said that he was going to do it. Dario and Chris ended up deciding to go to Google Brain. And so, it was really just, you know, Ilya, me, and, you know, John starting to be maybe few others. And so, I had a group of about 10 people that many of them were saying, I’m interested, but who else is in?

I asked Sam, okay, how do we break symmetry here? How do we actually get everyone to say, all right, we’re joining? And Sam’s suggestion was, invite people out for an offsite. So, we set up a thing in Napa, and I actually made t-shirts. And this is before they had joined. There was no official offers, no one had joined, we didn’t have a structure, we had nothing. Right? We just had an idea, we had a vision, we had a mission.

And we flew people out, we drove up to Napa together, and it was an amazing day. Right, the ideas were flowing. We came up with what I would really say is almost the technical plan that we’ve pursued for the past 10 years. Number one, solve reinforcement learning. Number two, solve unsupervised learning. And number three was gradually learn more complicated, in quotes, things. After that offsite, I sent offers to everyone and said, “Hey, we want to get started in the next two to three weeks.

0:04:25 — DeepMind’s Lead Over OpenAI

Greg Brockman: Please let me know if you’re in.”

Shane Parrish: Why did you think that DeepMind had such an insurmountable advantage?

Greg Brockman: It was very much the case that Google DeepMind was the 10,000-lb gorilla in the field. They just had lots of capital. They had the track record. This is before AlphaGo, right? AlphaGo came out a couple months later, but it wasn’t a surprise, right? It’s like very much the momentum was very clearly there.

0:04:54 — The Change from a Pure Non-Profit

Greg Brockman: And so, the question of is it really possible to build something independent and new, it wasn’t obvious.

Shane Parrish: At what point did you realize that like this nonprofit thing just wasn’t going to work?

Greg Brockman: In 2017, we started to think very hard about, first of all, how do we really achieve the mission? How do we actually build an AGI [artificial general intelligence]? What will that look like? And we started to do the math on compute, and you start to realize that it’s going to take big computer.

And we came across a company called Cerebras, which was building a unique piece of computing hardware. And that the kind of computer that they were promising, we realized was going to be far advanced of where our compute calculations looked.

And you start to realize if we could buy a lot of those computers, we could actually probably succeed at building an AGI. If we could get exclusive access to Cerebras, that could give us an overwhelming advantage. If we could buy very large data centers, that could be something unique as well.

And the thing about nonprofit fundraising is I think that there is essentially a cap to what is possible there. And so, Elon, Sam, Ilya, and I all agreed that the only path forward for OpenAI, the only path to achieve the mission, was to create a for-profit entity associated with OpenAI of some form.

Note

Editor’s note. This describes 2017 deliberations. OpenAI’s capped-profit subsidiary, OpenAI LP, was not created until March 2019; Elon Musk left OpenAI’s board in February 2018, before that structure existed, and has since disputed aspects of this account in litigation. And while Cerebras is framed here as the hardware that motivated the shift, OpenAI ultimately scaled on NVIDIA GPUs through its Microsoft/Azure partnership rather than on Cerebras silicon.

0:06:05 — Breakthrough Moments at OpenAI

Greg Brockman: And so, we were committed to that direction, and that is something that we knew was the only way to achieve the mission.

Shane Parrish: When was the moment that you realized everything was going to change for you? Was that Dota [1], or was it before then or after?

Greg Brockman: The way that OpenAI works is it’s a series of moments where you realize that it’s real now. And every time you think that you understand it, that it is really settled in for you, you realize that there is a new horizon you had not yet appreciated.

And so, along the way, I think that there was the initial launch. It was like, “Wow, we actually got a team together. Now we can pursue this mission.” But you show up at the office the next day, and you’re like, “Well, what do we do?” Right? We didn’t even have a whiteboard. Do you know, Ilya and John wanted to write something on a whiteboard. I was like, “I will get a whiteboard. That’s something I can do.”

Dota, we had our first big result. Right? That really was like, “Wow, we can actually accomplish something when we put our mind to it.” You can actually see all this compute coming together. You scale up the compute, you scale up the result.

There were multiple moments with the GPT series, and I remember actually an early moment was the unsupervised sentiment neuron paper [2]. Have you heard that one?

Shane Parrish: I’ve heard of it, but I haven’t read it.

Greg Brockman: Okay. Yes, that one’s That one’s an interesting one cuz it’s 2017, and it’s really the first time that we saw semantics arise from training on a language modeling objective. So, you train on learn the next character, predict the next character, and then suddenly you get a neural net that understands sentiment, understands if something is positive or negative. Much harder than it sounds. But that was a moment where you realize, “Wow, we are building machines that can learn semantics, not just where the commas are and where the nouns and verbs are, but it can really learn the meaning of sentences.”

You got to push that. And then, of course, when you see something like a I remember we were playing with it and someone asked, “Why is this thing not an AGI?” Right? It’s like actually really hard to put your finger on it cuz you can talk to it fluently in anything you want. It clearly wasn’t an AGI. It was lacking something, but just if you’d describe your criteria for AGI 2 months prior, it probably wouldn’t be compatible with what GPT-4 was.

And so there are many moments along the way where you feel like it’s real now. It’s going to really happen. The economy is going to transform into this compute-powered world. And I think that those moments are not yet at the end.

0:08:22 — What Dota 2 Meant for OpenAI

Greg Brockman: I think that we have many more breakthrough moments where you realize that the next stage is possible.

Shane Parrish: I thought Dota was like an incredible moment because it wasn’t chess like Deep Blue and it wasn’t AlphaGo, which is like computationally intensive but very defined rules. It was actually interactive against humans in a way that like the world is sort of structured, but you have all of this freedom.

Greg Brockman: Yeah, that was something very compelling about it. And the ironic thing is we’d actually set out with Dota to develop new methods because the reinforcement learning at the time was clearly not going to scale. Right? That the algorithm we use is called PPO [proximal policy optimization] [3]. You plan over every single time step. There’s no hierarchy. Whereas a human, that’s not how you plan your day. And so we knew that this algorithm was incredibly flawed, would never scale, and had all these problems.

But you got to start somewhere. You got to push your baselines to reach the wall so you actually see the limits of what good looks like with what you have and then you can bring to bear a new algorithm. And we just kept scaling PPO and we exceeded the performance of the best humans.

And that itself was the finding, right? That actually massive compute with simple algorithms. Right? That is something where we can not just doesn’t just work in theory. It works in practice. We can really make it happen. And in this incredibly messy environment where you cannot program it, you cannot look ahead, you cannot do a search, you just need this almost human-like intuition.

And by the way, the neuron that we used, tiny tiny little insect brain, similar number of synapses as to truly an insect brain. And you realize like, wait, what if you had the same computational approach, but scaled it up to something that’s much more human brain scale, what would that be like?

0:10:04 — Reasoning Versus Prediction

Greg Brockman: Very very evocative question.

Shane Parrish: Is there a difference between reasoning and predicting? You mentioned sort of like predicting the next character, predicting the next word versus actually reasoning in first principles.

Greg Brockman: I think they’re connected in a deep way. So, on the one hand, just predicting what comes next sounds like a pedestrian task. But if you really can predict the next word out of Einstein’s mouth, you are at least as smart as Einstein. And you can make arguments, oh, well, like, you know, it’s but I think that those arguments fall flat, that there’s something there’s something false there because the point of prediction is not about being able to predict what is known. The point is you put yourself in a new situation you’ve never seen before and predict what comes next. And I think that there’s something deeply connected to intelligence and prediction that there’s a long story of academic literature and how you think about this, compression, they’re all kind of part of the same thing.

Now, these reasoning models, the thing that I think is very interesting is that we train them with reinforcement learning. And so, there’s really back to the original OpenAI plan, there’s two steps to it. The first is unsupervised learning, you train a model just by having it predict what comes next, and there it’s much more static data, it’s much more observational. Again, it’s data it’s never seen before, situations never seen before, but it is a situation that is already happened.

Then you do reinforcement learning, which is you basically have the AI learn its own data, right? You have it make its own, here’s the action I’m going to take, you get an observation from the world, and you learn from that. And it’s again, the way you actually train it is still predicting. It’s trying to predict if I take this action, what’s the thing that’s likely to happen. And you reinforce that depending on how good of a job you did.

And the beauty of that is that it now is an AI that has this background knowledge and has real world experience. But fundamentally, the technology that we used to train during unsupervised stage and during the reinforcing stage, they’re exactly the same.

0:11:59 — Tensions Grow at OpenAI

Greg Brockman: You are just predicting, but you’ve changed the structure of the data.

Shane Parrish: When did things start to get tense?

Greg Brockman: I think the thing about OpenAI is that if you truly believe in the mission, if you truly believe in the possibility of creating machines that have the intelligence level of humans, it means the stakes always feel very high. The question of who’s making the decision, the question of what are the values that go into those decisions, the question of these things that are maybe mundane in a typical company that are much more like office politics, start to take on this existential weight.

And I think that has colored a lot of how OpenAI these more high high-profile conflicts, you know, sometimes it’s like you put it in like even just the question of who gets credit for a particular thing, it suddenly takes on this existential weight.

Shane Parrish: Well, that’s where I was sort of thinking of it this because it’s like at that point you probably realized this technology is inevitable and it’s going to change the world. And that wasn’t broadly known to the world. And then I would imagine there’s people who like I want to be front and center. I want to take credit for this.

Greg Brockman: Yes. That is the overwhelming dynamic that I have observed in this field. It’s not just about OpenAI actually. Like one observation I had early on is that this technology is by nature very fragmentary, right? That it’s sometimes it, you know, like when you have a lot of pressure, you can get a diamond or you can get cracks. Often you’ll see diamonds form in pockets, right? Teams of people that really work together, that have a lot of high trust, that know how to operate. But sometimes you can see that they splinter off and they kind of go their own way.

And I think within AI, I think we’ve gotten some real benefits out of diversity of approach and different groups that are really pushing each other in order to both bring this technology in a more beneficial way, sometimes how to think about all the thorny questions around safety, around what does it mean to be safe, what does it mean to actually deploy this technology, and how to think about how to mitigate and but also how to maximize those benefits.

And that’s something where I think that there’s a lot of very healthy debate. It’s always gone on within OpenAI’s walls. Now it’s starting to really happen, I think, in the world. And I think that’s something that we as a society really benefit from.

Shane Parrish: Take me back to the moment you found out that Sam had been fired. Where were you?

Greg Brockman: I was at home.

0:15:44 — Sam Altman’s Firing

Shane Parrish: And what happened?

Greg Brockman: I got a text saying, “Can we hop on a video call?” So, I hopped on the video call. I noticed that it was the board minus Sam who were on there.

Shane Parrish: Did you know at that point?

Greg Brockman: No. I mean, I inferred something was up.

Shane Parrish: But, cuz you’re on the board.

Greg Brockman: I am on the board. I was on the board.

Shane Parrish: At this point.

Greg Brockman: Yes.

Shane Parrish: And then what happened?

Greg Brockman: I was told that the board has decided that Sam would be removed. And effectively, the message that I got was the same messaging that was in the public post. And I asked if I could have any more information. I was told no, not right now. And I pressed on that, maybe another time. And again, was told nothing more to share.

And then was told, “Wait, there’s more.” Also, that I had been removed from the board, but would be staying with the company because I was very critical to the company and the mission. I said, again, I asked like any reasons, any feedback. Was told no.

Towards the end, was told that, “Hey, like in this new setup that you will start to get hopefully, you can get feedback in this new configuration.” And so, that was the conversation.

Note

Editor’s note. For the public timeline: the board removed Altman as CEO on November 17, 2023, and removed Brockman as chairman the same day. The reinstatement deal and Altman’s return were settled by around November 21–22, 2023.

Shane Parrish: What went through your mind?

Greg Brockman: It just wasn’t right.

Shane Parrish: Was it anger?

Greg Brockman: No. I felt like I understood what had happened.

Shane Parrish: How long before you knew what had actually transpired to sort of cause this?

Greg Brockman: Well, there’s two parts to the answer. One is I feel like I still am learning some additional facts, some additional thing that was in someone’s head. To some extent it comes down to a lack of communication, right? That you realize that there are all these different things that have buffered. And to some extent, you know, approximately I kind of knew.

0:17:49 — Greg Quits OpenAI

Greg Brockman: I was like, I understand for every person here, I have a pretty good model of why they acted the way that they did, but it wasn’t what was most important to me in the moment. I just knew that this wasn’t right. Right after I hung up the call, I talked to my wife and I said, “Got to quit.” And she said, “I agree.”

Shane Parrish: And you quit that day.

Greg Brockman: Yes.

Shane Parrish: And then what happened?

Greg Brockman: That day when I quit, I started to get all these messages of people saying, “I don’t know what you and Sam are doing next, but I’m with you. I want to go start something with you.” Like just that was a real honest surprise. I didn’t really expect to get that kind of support, that kind of outpouring.

There were a few of my close collaborators who quit that day as well. That’s Jakub, Szymon, Aleksander, and the five of us, so those people plus Sam, we all got together and we started to chart out what a new company could look like. I remember feeling that first day like, “Okay, there’s a 10% chance that we actually get the company back, 10%.”

The next day, we set up a meeting at Sam’s house. A bunch of people from the company came by and we showed the vision that we’d been sketching out. So it was just really one day in, you know, with this fresh picture of how we’d run the project and we spent that a bunch of time over that weekend also negotiating with the board and the company and trying to figure out is there a path back together that makes sense.

That Sunday night, the board replaced Mira as interim CEO with a new person and the company just rebelled. Like we’d actually been at the office, we thought we were close to a deal, and to come back. Yeah, we thought that we had a path. And then the board made that change, and then suddenly it was everyone streaming out of the building, and it was just like real chaos.

I was on video calls with many of the people who had been interested in coming to this new company saying it’s going to be okay, we have a plan, and we expanded, you know, we’d been building this little life raft, right, for the small set of people we expected to want to come.
