And even for example one of my friends was describing that his sister was describing this app that she really wished someone had created, that she had this picture of like exactly what she wanted. And he in the meanwhile was typing into Codex, uh-huh, uh-huh, and then pushed enter. And a few hours later, he shows her this app. And she’s like, “Wait, what is this? Like where did this thing come from? Who built this?” And he said “You did.” And that is I think just an amazing thing where you realize anyone can be a builder. Like these tools at Codex is for everyone. It’s not just for software engineers. It’s like everyone now can be a software engineer if they have a vision, if they have this agency that they have a thing that they want to accomplish. Like you now have this magic tool that can do it.

And then on the consumer side the thing about consumers it’s too broad of a term. Right? That there’s lots of different things. There’s like entertainment, there’s a bunch of things in self-expression, and there’s also solving goals. And the aspect of consumer that we’re really dialed in on is solving goals. Like we believe that this technology you’ll get smartphones. That’s like 4 billion people use them. All those people should have a personal AI, a personal AGI that’s out there that knows them well, that has their personal context that is trustworthy that they can ask for advice, but that also knows them so well that you know, if your favorite musician is in town, it just goes and proactively purchases tickets and maybe it knows like, oh, I should check in before doing this or maybe it knows, yep, that just like I got to get do this and I have I prior approval. Like that level of having an AI that knows you and can help you achieve whatever it is you want to achieve and help you flush out what are your goals. You should still set those goals. They should be your goals. Right, you should be in charge, but that is something we want to create and that is something I think that not just 4 billion people are going to want and need. I think it’s going to be 8 billion people. I think that the whole planet is going to really benefit from and need access to a personal AI, personal AGI.

And so you look at those two dimensions of the knowledge work and broad distribution of access to energetic system and we want to build those two aspects and they come together because ultimately they’re the same technology. Ultimately you want an AI that is there in the cloud that has access to information that is trustworthy, that is able to give good answers and able to take actions on your behalf.

0:53:05 — Data Centers in Space?

Greg Brockman: Whether it’s building, whether it’s in your personal life and maybe you have multiple instances of it, but fundamentally it is one technological system.

Shane Parrish: Do you think we’ll have data centers in space?

Greg Brockman: I think we’re going to have data centers everywhere.

Shane Parrish: How far away do you think we are from that?

Greg Brockman: Well, data centers in space has a lot of has many technical problems associated with it. Even for example, the data centers we build today are very finicky. Right, they’re these massive machines with very breakable, very expensive components. We’ve had many issues in the past where the cables were just too taut, just literally like two two tight of cables and then you get signal integrity issues and the computer doesn’t work.

And so figuring out how do you maintain systems today? It’s people go and physically them. Probably will move to robotics. So, I think figuring out how to solve some of these technical problems are going to be very important dependencies as we think about putting them in you know, you people talk about putting data center in, you know, various difficult locations.

Um space feels like a grand challenge, but I think that we have going to have such need for compute that we need to be thinking about all options.

Shane Parrish: What is iterative deployment and why do you do it?

Greg Brockman: Well, iterative deployment is one of the core pillars of how OpenAI has approached how to get this technology to benefit people and to achieve our mission. And this is something that I think I was probably the person who articulated those two words. But this spirit is something that really emerged as we thought about our first product deployment and really thinking about how does that connect to what we’re trying to do.

And you realize that there were two different routes that you could take in terms of thinking about the you want to build an AGI that’s going to benefit people, how do you do it? And one is you go for kind of build it in secret. You don’t deploy anything. You have a lot of time to just kind of polish it, get it right. But then at some point you push a button and you say deploy. And I remember thinking about could I sign up for that strategy? Could I be accountable for that strategy? Do you want to be sitting in a room thinking about, okay, we ran all our tests. Are we ready to deploy? And you’ve never deployed anything ever before. Right? That’s your first contact with reality. And it’s a very powerful system that’s going to really change the world. Like that is a very tough problem set.

But instead, what about if you take an approach where this is your hundredth system. You’ve had to solve this problem 99 times before with systems of increasing power. And the world has also had a chance to adapt to them, to reconfigure around them.

And we learned very early on with GPT-3. We got to see this very concretely what it’s like to deploy something where we spent a lot of time thinking about what are all the misuses of GPT-3, what are the ways it could go wrong. We thought about misinformation, we thought about these kinds of, you know, grand pictures. And you know what the number one misuse of GPT-3 was?

Shane Parrish: What?

Greg Brockman: It was medical spam, like advertising different drugs to people. Right? It’s like not something we ever would have thought of as a problem,

Shane Parrish: [clears throat]

Greg Brockman: but we see it in front of our eyes and we get a chance to react and learn from it. And so iterative deployment is the idea that we will bring intermediate intermediate versions of this technology.

Now, it’s not an excuse to just blindly deploy, right? You still need to think at every step about what’s our best view on all the ways this might be misused, what are the downsides, what are the risks?

Let’s mitigate those, but you get to see it. You get to see if you’re right, learn from reality, and do better the next time.

Shane Parrish: I think people don’t understand the extent of which like this is all new. There’s no playbook. Like you’re figuring this out as you go as well on the most rapidly deployed technology in the world perhaps that’s so powerful.

Greg Brockman: It is true that at various points in OpenAI’s history, we’ve had some hope that, “Hey, there are people who have deployed transformative technologies before. Maybe they can tell us the answers.” And it’s never been so simple. They do have wisdom and insights, and that’s something that I think we’ve really incorporated, but we realized that we’re the closest ones to this technology. That by virtue of creating it, we have an understanding of the ways in which we could shape it. That is hard for someone who isn’t so close to it to opine on, to advise on.

And I think that one observation I have is that the right choices are extremely specific to the facts of the technology. There’s different pressures that are exerted by cell phones versus, you know, mainframe computers versus AI versus electricity. Each one of these has its own unique proclivities and problems. That’s ways that they’re being developed. The individuals doing it matter too, right? The dynamics between different humans and these human factors have been hugely impactful for how AI is playing out today in front of our eyes.

I think that a lot of what we spend our time doing from the beginning of OpenAI and really even before is you spend a lot of time dreaming. You spend a lot of time really thinking about all the implications of what you might do.

And I think that one thing I’ve observed is that we haven’t really been surprised by some moments along the way, but we have been surprised by when they arrive, how hard they are to accomplish, exactly the order in which we see them. And that the world that we are moving towards is I think one that is in many ways more wonderful and awe-inspiring than many of the ones we anticipated.

Shane Parrish: If one frontier model puts safety as a primary concern and another frontier model doesn’t, how do you view that competition playing out over time?

Greg Brockman: Well, I think we have found that safety is actually a core product feature. Like no one wants a model that is not aligned with them. Right? You want a model you can trust that does the right things in any circumstance you give it. And so we have invested I think we’ve actually invested possibly far more than certainly people perceive and possibly more than any other lab in safety, right?

That we have in ChatGPT the broadest deployment of AI these language models in the world used by the most people. We have to care. We’ve always cared, but you really see it in terms of us being able to bring this technology to so many people. So I don’t think that there’s a sustainable state where the people who are building this technology and having successful products are not also investing super hard in safety.

And I think that actually the challenge is a little bit about if you step back, because there are some aspects of what it means to deliver safety that are not necessarily short-term. You have to think long-term for your not just your business, but for what it is that you’re creating. And some of this is about how you train the models, some of this is about how do you get your feedback loop. But I would just say that we are committed to safety as part of our mission, and that’s something where I think it has played out in our products and in the world.

One thing that people also miss is that it’s not just about the safety of the model, it’s about the resilience of society. If you look at how transformative technologies enter the world, that society builds around them about their strengths and their risks. You think about engines, right? You build cars, but you also need seat belts, you also need to have roads, and you reorient cities around the fact of this is how this technology works. You think about electricity, you have various safety standards, you have different kinds of where you’re allowed to put the electric poles, right? And high-voltage lines and all these things. And I think the same will be true for AI, that it’s not just about the technology itself, it’s not about the model itself. It’s really about how do they integrate into the world with a society that is resilient. And that is something we’re investing in very significantly.

1:00:56 — What Should AI Regulation Look Like?

Greg Brockman: The OpenAI Foundation has this as one of its key focuses of trying to help society invest in and build a resilient layer for AI.

Shane Parrish: What do you think regulation for AI should look like?

Greg Brockman: Well, I think that there’s a number of different pieces to what regulation for AI needs to accomplish. One I think is very important is we need to ultimately ensure this technology benefits people. And you think about questions like it is very clear that institutions, jobs, just life paths that people thought would be stable, those assumptions may not hold anymore. And we need to make sure that we provide support, that we’re all there to support each other as this technology rolls out.

And so, what does that mean from a regulatory perspective? I think there’s a lot of ideas, whether it’s things like everyone should have access to compute. How do we ensure that’s true? How do we ensure that as this technology starts to generate more economic value, that it doesn’t accrue to just one place, right? This should be something that actually everyone is benefiting from. This technology shouldn’t just abstractly benefit the economy, it’s very clearly going to do. It should directly be something that people feel in their daily lives, that they themselves, their life is better because this technology exists, because they’re using it, because they’re able to accomplish more.

And I think that the ways in which I see this playing out, it’s very important to ground it in what are we really seeing. Like a good example is the number of people whose who say that their life, or their life was saved, or the life of a loved one was saved through the use of ChatGPT. And you realize that’s something that should be supported and protected. And so, a good example of how you can do that through regulation is thinking about privacy and privilege. You talk to a doctor, you talk to a lawyer, those are privileged conversations, right? You feel comfortable sharing them. There’s certain guardrails on when the health care provider would have to, you know, provide that information to law enforcement or alert someone. Well defined in the law. We don’t have anything like that for AI right now. But people are using these tools, and they should use these tools because they’re so important for giving people access to information that they wouldn’t be able to get otherwise, and that they should have the appropriate kind of understanding and protections there, too.

And so, I think that there’s a lot of just really leaning into thinking about how do these models insert into people’s lives? How do we make sure that we can continue to innovate, while at the same time, also making sure that the benefits flow broadly. How do we ensure that America remains a leader, right? That you think about robotics, where I think we are not the leader. I think that for AI, we have to make sure that we continue with this remarkable position that [clears throat] we have been able to achieve. And you think about things like data centers, that those are something where there’s clearly been a lot of concern about questions like do they drive up electricity prices? And we have a commitment to ensure that they do not. And I think that each of these things can be achieved through many different mechanisms. Sometimes it’s through regulation, sometimes it’s through commitments from the company, and sometimes it’s just through people understanding the facts. Like a good example is data centers and water usage. Like that’s something that people talk about a lot, but actually our data centers use incredibly little water, right? That’s actually misinformation that they use a lot.

Shane Parrish: It’s less than a household, isn’t it?

Greg Brockman: It’s It is, because it’s a closed loop. You basically fill up a giant like, you know, think of it as like a swimming pool of water, and you just circle it around. And so it’s a fixed amount of water that’s not very large, but I think people really understanding the why. Why are we building these things? Why is it worthwhile? How does it benefit me?

1:04:33 — The Future of AI-Powered Entrepreneurship

Greg Brockman: And being able to give people that empowerment, whether it’s helping them feel that they can be an entrepreneur now, that they can build a business, that they can create something. Like all of that we have to solve for.

1:04:44 — AI and Job Loss

Greg Brockman: We have to make sure that people feel it in their daily lives.

Note

Editor’s note. Data-center water use is contested. Closed-loop liquid cooling recirculates its working fluid, but large facilities still consume water through evaporative cooling and through the electricity they draw; independent estimates vary widely by site and cooling design.

Shane Parrish: When I told people I was doing this interview, one of the common reactions is that they’re fearing for their job and their uncertainty. What would you tell them?

Greg Brockman: Well, I do think that this technology it is uncertain exactly how it will play out. I think it is surprising how it will play out as well. Like the AIs that we have right now, the world that we have right now, is not really something that was anticipated by science fiction. It’s just different. And some inevitable conclusions, I think, actually turn out to not quite look the same way when they come to pass.

So, I believe it’s always easiest to see what you lose. Right? And the change is coming. There’s no denying that. That is absolutely the case. But, it’s much harder to see a priori what you gain. And as an example, just think about Uber. If you describe it to someone in 1950, you have to think about computers. You have to think about mobile phones. You have to think about GPS. And it’s all so that you can get a car to appear where you are in 3 minutes. And like that’s actually crazy if you think about that level of technological investment for that kind of use case. But, it really happened. And it didn’t just happen for that one use case. It happened for thousands, for tens of thousands, for millions of other use cases.

And so, I think that my view of AI is it is about empowerment. It is about human agency. And that does mean that some of these institutions, jobs, these kinds of things that there will be things that we thought we could rely on that turn out not to be as stable as we thought. And so, it will affect people. But, the question to lean into is what do you gain and how do you benefit from it? So, now you can be a builder. You can create anything anything you can imagine can become real.

Well, what do you imagine? How do you build that skill? Really leaning into this technology. Like one thing that I have observed is across multiple generations of this technology, the people who seem to be getting the most benefit out of it are the people who did it for the previous one. Right? So, the more that you build the skill and at the core of it is agency, is having a vision, is having ideas. Because now the barrier to entry to trying them out is lower than ever before. So, I think there will be new opportunity created. I think that the world does need to think about how do we support everyone through this moment of uncertainty, through whatever transitions will come. Because the economy will be a compute power economy. It will be different, but I think that there will be a place for everyone to contribute.

1:07:15 — The Skills Young People Should Invest In

Shane Parrish: Where should young people be investing today? If you’re in high school or university or just trying to start out in a job, what skills do you think will be more valuable in the future?

Greg Brockman: Well, I really think leaning into this technology is going to be a critical skill. Just really understanding how do you get the most out of AI? Because we’re all going to be heading to a world where we’re managers of agents, and soon maybe the CEO of an autonomous AI corporation. Or just imagine if you had the workforce of you know, a 100,000 person company all at your disposal, operating on your behalf.

Shane Parrish: 24/7.

Greg Brockman: 24/7, right? As long as you’ve got the tokens, the compute to power it, which again I think everyone needs access to compute. That’s like so critical for the world to figure out and get right.

Because then at that point you can point that at any problem. And the number of problems that humanity could want to solve are boundless.

And so I think that the more the people do lean into this technology, figure out how to take advantage of what’s coming, how to combine these technologies in new ways, how to interact with our agents to really manage them, to think about when what is it that I want, what is it that is my sense of self, what is my purpose, what do I want to see in the world, it is going to be easier than ever to accomplish that. And I think that world, the what we gain, I think is going to be almost unimaginable in its upside.

Shane Parrish: That’s the most positive sort of view of the future. What’s the most negative one you can imagine?

Greg Brockman: One thing that’s very interesting about how technology has played out to date is that it’s really been about contorting ourselves to the machine. Right? You think about how many people work where you have this box and you’re typing away at it and you’re getting your carpal tunnel and your shoulders are hunched and all of those things that were not natural, right? That’s not really what we’re designed for.

And we’re going to be moving to this world where it’s not just that you’re doing work with your computer, so your computer actually does work for you. And that is something that presents opportunities. I think it presents risks. I think we need to figure out how to mitigate those. Like one core thing at the end of the day is that if you have machines that help people actualize their goals, right? That’s out there doing what you want. Sometimes people have conflicting goals. How do you resolve that? How do you decide what the bounds are on what an AI will help you with and what they won’t?

Really trying to figure out how does this slot into society? How do you make sure that the benefits don’t just go to one corporation, one set of people, but that actually do lift up everyone. We need to raise the floor so that everyone has access to a great life, this technology, and are able to do things with it. And I think it’ll correspondingly also lift the ceiling. And so I think we’re going to be in a world where everyone is going to have new opportunities, that there will be more just I don’t know if the right word is safety net or just like that there should be something that really is able to make sure that everyone gets brought along. But then we’re going to be able to accomplish so much more.

And you think about things like access to medical care. Like we should be in a world, if we do our job right, where everyone gets access, has a doctor in their pocket that is better than any team of doctors today. The world’s best doctors, they’re there for you. They care about you. They’re actually reading your charts, that they’re thinking 24/7 about how can we actually help with this condition? It’s disruptive, right? It’s not going to come for free in terms of how this technology will interact with the world, and we’ve already seen the beginning errors of it. But, I think that what we’re going to see over just even the next 2 years, I think it will be this force for good, but we have to also acknowledge all the ways that it could go wrong or the risks of it in order to achieve those upsides.

1:11:30 — What Does Success Look Like For You?

Shane Parrish: We always end every podcast with the same question, which is what is success for you?

Greg Brockman: Achieving the OpenAI mission of ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity.

Shane Parrish: Thank you very much. This was awesome.

Greg Brockman: This is a great conversation, man.

References

Talk and source

  • YouTube video (~72 min; The Knowledge Project, episode page)
  • Episode page — Farnam Street (full written transcript is members-only)

People

  • Greg Brockman — OpenAI cofounder and president
  • Shane Parrish — host, The Knowledge Project
  • Sam Altman, Ilya Sutskever, Dario Amodei, Chris Olah, John Schulman, Elon Musk, Mira Murati, Satya Nadella, Patrick Collison

Companies and products

  • OpenAI — ChatGPT, Codex
  • Stripe, Google DeepMind, Google Brain, Cerebras, Arc Institute

Concepts and background

  • Artificial general intelligence, reinforcement learning, unsupervised learning, knowledge distillation
  • AlphaGo, Deep Blue

Papers and technical reports

  1. Berner, C., Brockman, G., Chan, B., et al. “Dota 2 with Large Scale Deep Reinforcement Learning.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:1912.06680), December 13, 2019. https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.06680
  2. Radford, A., Jozefowicz, R., Sutskever, I. “Learning to Generate Reviews and Discovering Sentiment.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:1704.01444), April 5, 2017. https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01444
  3. Schulman, J., Wolski, F., Dhariwal, P., Radford, A., Klimov, O. “Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:1707.06347), July 20, 2017. https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347

  • Sutskever at NeurIPS 2024: Pre-Training Era Is Over: a counterweight to Brockman’s claim that pretraining and reasoning run on the same prediction machinery, from the cofounder whose departure he calls his hardest moment.

item.title: Superintelligence: The Idea That Eats Smart People
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In a 2016 talk at Web Camp Zagreb, Maciej Cegłowski, who runs the bookmarking service Pinboard, argues that belief in machine superintelligence is “the idea that eats smart people”: a chain of individually plausible premises that, followed to the end, turns capable engineers into a quasi-religious movement. He opens with the 1945 worry that the first atomic-bomb test might set the atmosphere on fire, a fear physicists could rule out because the underlying nuclear laws were well understood, and uses it as the foil for the AI version of the same fear: a “runaway reaction” in which a machine reaches and then exceeds human intelligence in a very short span. His target is Nick Bostrom’s Superintelligence, the 2014 book that synthesizes the alarmist case and that Stephen Hawking, Elon Musk, and a raft of Silicon Valley investors found persuasive.

The premises. The talk first lays out the six assumptions Bostrom’s intelligence-explosion argument needs:

  • Proof of concept: thinking minds exist, so the thing is possible in principle.
  • No quantum shenanigans: the brain is ordinary matter that could be emulated, with no quantum magic required (contra Roger Penrose).
  • Many possible minds: the space of possible minds is large, and no physical law caps intelligence at the human level. A motorcycle outruns any cheetah, but evolution had to build humans first before anything could build the motorcycle.
  • Plenty of room at the top: hardware still has room to get much smaller and faster.
  • Computer-like time scales: software would run on machine time scales, vastly faster than human thought.
  • Recursive self-improvement: an AI could improve itself, looping into a runaway takeoff.

The rebuttals. He then attacks the takeoff scenario from about a dozen angles, most named for a memorable image:

  • “Intelligence” has no agreed definition, and may not even be a single quantity you can maximize.
  • Stephen Hawking’s cat: a huge intelligence advantage doesn’t let Hawking talk a cat into its carrier, and a disembodied AI has the same problem, it must persuade humans to act for it. Einstein’s cat and the Australian Emu War extend the point: even brute force, or coordinated humans with machine guns, can be defeated by far less intelligent creatures.
  • Slavic Pessimism: we can’t write secure software (he cites an Ethereum contract that was exploited to drain tens of millions), so expecting to code a stable moral fixed point that survives thousands of rounds of self-modification, correctly, on the first try, doesn’t match any experience we have.
  • Complex Motivations: against the Orthogonality Thesis and its paperclip maximizer, he argues that complex minds probably have complex motivations, and would sooner write poetry about paperclips than tile the universe with them.
  • The Argument From Actual AI: real progress comes from pouring massive amounts of data into relatively simple, opaque neural networks, which offer no place to recursively tweak short of retraining on more data.
  • The roommate, brain surgery, childhood, and Gilligan’s Island arguments push the same way: raw intelligence doesn’t imply a drive to self-improve or conquer, it is massively interconnected rather than a tunable module, it develops slowly through interaction with the world, and it is distributed across an entire civilization rather than sitting in one mind.

The outside arguments. The second half is about what believing all this does to a culture:

  • Grandiosity: enormous payoffs multiplied by tiny probabilities, used to justify almost anything.

  • Megalomania: fixing the world by building a God-machine. The talk quotes Joi Ito on the people doing it:

    This may upset some of my students at MIT, but one of my concerns is that it’s been a predominantly male gang of kids, mostly white, who are building the core computer science around AI, and they’re more comfortable talking to computers than to human beings. A lot of them feel that if they could just make that science-fiction, generalized AI, we wouldn’t have to worry about all the messy stuff like politics and society. They think machines will just figure it all out for us.

  • Religion 2.0: the singularity as a nerd apocalypse offering immortality and even resurrection.

  • Comic-book ethics: a few lone heroes charged with saving the world, an industry of rich men who think they are Batman.

  • Simulation fever: the same reasoning, taken far enough, concludes we already live in a simulation.

  • Data hunger: the surveillance economy as a byproduct of data-hungry AI.

  • AI cosplay: people behaving like their own fantasy of a hyperintelligent agent.

His own position: our understanding of the mind is roughly where alchemy was in the 1600s, diligent but missing the key tools, and the pressing risks are mundane, people exploiting people, carelessness baked into automated systems, and surveillance, not a machine takeover.

My Notes

  • Ito’s demographic claim held up. The talk quotes Joi Ito on AI being built by a “predominantly male” and “mostly white” group, which in 2016 sounds like an offhand provocation. The measurements that came soon after support it. Nesta’s study of arXiv AI papers found only 13.8% of authors are women, with no improvement in the share of woman-authored papers since the 1990s. The AI Now Institute’s Discriminating Systems report counted women as 18% of authors at major AI conferences and more than 80% of AI professors as men, and put Black workers at 2.5% of Google’s staff and 4% at Facebook and Microsoft. Both are 2019 figures, but because that share had been flat for decades, the imbalance Ito named looks structural rather than a snapshot. More recent workforce counts run somewhat higher, though women remain a clear minority of AI researchers.

Related Posts

  • Recursive Superintelligence’s $4B Bet on Self-Improving AI: the recursive self-improvement the talk rebutted in 2016 is now a funded category, a $4B+ lab betting on automating AI research itself.
  • Yann LeCun on What Comes After LLMs: another skeptic who calls LLMs a dead end for human-level intelligence and locates the danger in mundane failure modes rather than a takeover, the same split the talk draws.
  • Karpathy: AGI Is Still a Decade Away: a working researcher’s version of the “Argument From Actual AI,” doubtful that models training on their own outputs lead anywhere but collapse.
  • Math Is AGI: Carina Hong on Axiom and Formal Reasoning: the believer side, a commercial pitch treating AGI as both imminent and the most important thing to build, the conviction the talk calls grandiosity.

item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:

In Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness [1] (ICML 1999), Volodya Vovk, Alex Gammerman, and Craig Saunders at Royal Holloway, University of London unify their earlier transduction work into a single scheme based on the notion of algorithmic randomness — one of the founding papers of what is now called conformal prediction. The complaint that opens the paper is that most learning algorithms output a bare prediction with no measure of how much to trust it, and that the example a classifier is least sure about is exactly the one a user most needs flagged.

The paper rests on two quantities, and the rest of it is about how to compute them. Each candidate label gets a p-value measuring how well that labeling fits the training data. The across labels are separate tail probabilities, one per candidate-label hypothesis, not a distribution over labels, and they need not sum to 1. The prediction is the label with the largest p-value, :

  • Confidence , where is the second-largest p-value across the candidate labels. High confidence means every label other than the predicted one fits the data poorly, so the prediction is unlikely to be wrong at the corresponding error level.
  • Credibility , how well the best available label fits the data at all. Low credibility flags an input unlike anything in the training set: either the data are not exchangeable or the test example is unrepresentative, regardless of how confident the prediction looks.

The pair separates two failure modes that a single probability hides. A prediction can be confident but have low credibility — a signal that the input itself is strange, not just that the label is uncertain.

The abstract

Most machine learning algorithms share the following drawback: they only output bare predictions but not the confidence in those predictions. In the 1960s algorithmic information theory supplied universal measures of confidence but these are, unfortunately, non-computable. In this paper we combine the ideas of algorithmic information theory with the theory of Support Vector machines to obtain practicable approximations to universal measures of confidence. We show that in some standard problems of pattern recognition our approximations work well.

Methods

The construction has three layers, and only the third one runs on a computer.

The ideal, non-computable target. A p-value function, or randomness level, scores how well a data sequence fits the independent-and-identically-distributed (iid) assumption: large when the sequence looks like a typical iid draw, small when it contains a pattern an iid source would rarely produce. (“Random” here is the algorithmic sense of “indistinguishable from a fair-coin sample,” not the colloquial “erratic.”) To classify a test point , the ideal algorithm tries every candidate label, completes the sequence , and measures the randomness level of each completion. It predicts the label whose completion has the largest randomness level, — the label that makes the data look most consistent with iid, hence the least anomalous. Credibility is that largest randomness level, , and confidence is one minus the second-largest, .

The second-largest is what matters because the valid prediction set at significance level is , and this is the single label only when every alternative is rejected. That is an AND across the other labels, so the binding constraint is the largest of their p-values: . So is the highest confidence at which the predictor commits to one label. The error guarantee falls out of validity: each is a genuine p-value, so under the hypothesis that is correct, and because a wrong prediction means the true label is the rejected one, it has probability at most . Credibility plays the complementary role: a small means even the best label is atypical, flagging the input rather than the label.

The trouble is that the universal measures of randomness from Kolmogorov [2] and Martin-Löf [3] are non-computable — they can be approximated from below but never evaluated exactly.

The Support Vector approximation. To get something computable, the paper borrows Vapnik’s Support Vector Machine (SVM) [4]. Solving the SVM’s dual optimization assigns each example a Lagrange multiplier that grows with how hard the example is to fit. The earlier “Learning by Transduction” paper (Gammerman, Vapnik, and Vovk [5]) turned multipliers into a score with . The companion paper (Saunders, Gammerman, and Vovk [6]) turns them into a p-value by ranking: sort the multipliers in decreasing order, and the p-value of a completion is the rank of the test example’s multiplier divided by . A genuinely strange or mislabelled example earns a large multiplier, ends up near the top of the ranking, and so gets a small p-value.

The experiment. The test bed is United States Postal Service (USPS) handwritten digits (LeCun et al. [7]), each a image, with a two-class problem separating the digit 2 from the digit 7. The classifier is an SVM with a degree-3 polynomial kernel , trained on 400 examples and evaluated on 100 single-example test sets.

Results

  • Confidence and credibility separate correct from incorrect predictions (Figure 2, credibility on the vertical axis, confidence on the horizontal). With , the 100 predictions split into two clusters by average credibility: a cluster of 93 correct examples is at credibility 1.0 and average confidence 0.902, while the cluster holding the single error (plus 6 correct examples) is at credibility 0.091. Credibility, not confidence, is what marks the examples the classifier should not be trusted on.
  • The choice of score function matters. The rule from the transduction paper suffers a “distortion phenomenon” and predicts worse. Switching to or pushes average confidence above 0.99 on the correct cluster while keeping the error cluster’s credibility low.
  • The error bound is . For a single test example, the randomness deficiency of a wrongly-labelled sequence is at most , and the paper notes this matches the denominator in Vapnik’s statistical learning theory and in PAC-style error bounds — the same quantity obtained from the algorithmic-randomness side.

The paper closes with a set of impossibility results (Section 6). Under the iid assumption alone:

  • On-line prediction at every step is impossible (§6.1). If both the data sequence and the stopping time are random, inequality (9) shows that even the wrong labeled sequence has a random continuation under iid — so under iid alone there is no way to rule out wrong predictions at a randomly chosen time. The paper offers this as the technical explanation for why machine learning under iid has stayed in the batch setting. Practical impact: conformal prediction’s coverage guarantee holds at fixed batches, not at adversarially chosen stopping times. Streaming pipelines that need valid coverage at every step need assumptions stronger than iid.
  • Density estimation in high dimensions is impossible (§6.2). When the input dimension is large compared to the sample size, the unlabelled are typically all distinct. Under iid, for any generating distribution there is a degenerate that places entirely on or for each but is indistinguishable from on the sample. So cannot be estimated to anything narrower than without strictly stronger assumptions. Practical impact: conformal prediction returns a prediction set (the true label is among these) rather than a calibrated per-class probability like . The latter is provably out of reach in high dimensions under iid alone.
  • Regression as conditional-expectation estimation reduces to density estimation (§6.3). Estimating under iid coincides with density estimation in the binary case, so the §6.2 impossibility transfers. Under a different framing, where are deterministic and only are stochastic, even pattern recognition becomes impossible without additional assumptions. Practical impact: conformal regression methods deliver prediction intervals (a calibrated band around ) rather than calibrated point estimates of , for the same reason.

What came after

The scheme here is transductive — to score a test example it effectively retrains for every candidate label, which is expensive — and the nonconformity signal is tied to the SVM. The work that followed relaxed both.

  • The general form. Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer’s Algorithmic Learning in a Random World [8] consolidated the theory into a form where any nonconformity score, not just an SVM multiplier, drives the calibration.
  • Split conformal prediction. Papadopoulos et al. [9] replaced the per-label retraining with a single held-out calibration set, cheap enough to wrap around any pre-trained model — the form most practitioners use today.
  • Workarounds for the impossibility results. Each of the §6 impossibilities has a follow-up that recovers what is possible without violating the underlying constraint:
    • On-line prediction (§6.1): Adaptive Conformal Inference (Gibbs and Candès [13]) updates the conformal threshold over time, holding long-run coverage under distribution shift. The new guarantee is a long-run coverage rate rather than per-step validity, which is why the §6.1 impossibility does not apply.
    • Density estimation in high dimensions (§6.2): Venn–Abers predictors (Vovk and Petej [11]) output a calibrated probability interval rather than a single number. An interval is what is achievable under iid alone in high dimensions, where the §6.2 impossibility blocks single-number probabilities.
    • Regression (§6.3): Conformalized quantile regression (Romano, Patterson, and Candès [10]) reformulates the task as quantile estimation and returns calibrated, locally adaptive prediction intervals. The impossibility blocks point estimates of , not interval coverage, so quantile regression sidesteps it.
  • The deep-learning revival. Angelopoulos and Bates’ tutorial [12] repackaged the framework for deep learning and drove the recent wave of distribution-free uncertainty work — including the conformal factuality and conformal language modeling methods built for language models.

My Notes

  • The middle layer is the IJCAI companion paper. This paper has three layers (ideal non-computable target, computable SVM approximation, experiment), and the middle layer comes from the same trio’s IJCAI 1999 paper [6] on transduction with confidence and credibility. That paper introduces the SVM-rank-of-multipliers construction standalone, while this one wraps the same construction in algorithmic-randomness theory and adds the impossibility results.
  • Mapping to LLM prediction. The paper picks the predicted label via and exposes the value at that argmax as credibility, . LLM token prediction does the same operation, , with the max softmax as the value at the argmax. So when an LLM is described as “95% confident in its prediction,” that 95% is colloquially called confidence but is structurally the paper’s credibility. The paper’s confidence (, one minus the second-largest p-value) is a different number with no common LLM analog. Wrapping conformal prediction around the LLM uses as the nonconformity score on a held-out calibration set, and the result has the coverage guarantee the raw max softmax lacks.

item.title: Transduction with Confidence and Credibility
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Transduction with Confidence and Credibility [1] (IJCAI 1999), Craig Saunders, Alex Gammerman, and Vladimir Vovk at Royal Holloway, University of London build a transductive classifier on top of a Support Vector Machine (SVM) that, for each new example, returns not just a label but two numbers describing how much to trust it. The numbers come from p-values, and the construction is the direct ancestor of conformal prediction.

The paper rests on two quantities, and the rest of it is about how to compute them. Each candidate label gets a p-value measuring how strange the test point looks against the training set under the hypothesis that its label is . The prediction is the label with the largest p-value, :

  • Confidence , where is the second-largest p-value across the candidate labels. High confidence means the runner-up label is firmly rejected, so the prediction is unlikely to be wrong at the corresponding error level.
  • Credibility , how well the best available label fits the training set at all. Low credibility flags an input unlike anything in the training set: the test point is strange under every hypothesis, regardless of how confident the prediction looks.

The split matters because the two can disagree. A prediction can be 99% confident and 1% credible: every alternative label is rejected, yet the winning label is also a poor fit. The paper’s Table 1 shows three such cases: handwritten digits with high-confidence wrong answers that credibility correctly flags as untrustworthy.

The abstract

In this paper we follow the same general ideology as in [Gammerman et al., 1998], and describe a new transductive learning algorithm using Support Vector Machines. The algorithm presented provides confidence values for its predicted classifications of new examples. We also obtain a measure of “credibility” which serves as an indicator of the reliability of the data upon which we make our prediction. Experiments compare the new algorithm to a standard Support Vector Machine and other transductive methods which use Support Vector Machines, such as Vapnik’s margin transduction. Empirical results show that the new algorithm not only produces confidence and credibility measures, but is comparable to, and sometimes exceeds the performance of the other algorithms.

Methods

Induction learns a general rule from the training set and then applies it to any future point. Transduction skips the general rule and reasons straight from the training examples to the specific test point in front of it. The paper’s recipe is to fold the test point into the training set under a tentative label, fit an SVM to the combined data, and ask how unusual the test point looks once it is in there.

The measure of “unusual” is the strangeness of an example, and it reuses a quantity the SVM already produces. After fitting, every example in the training set (now including the test point) carries a Lagrange multiplier . An near zero means the example is on the correct side of the margin and contributes nothing to the boundary. A large means the example is hard to fit: it lands on or inside the margin and influences the boundary. So a large marks a strange, poorly supported point, and a small marks an ordinary one.

Strangeness on its own is just a number on an arbitrary scale. To turn it into something comparable across examples, the paper ranks the test point’s multiplier against all the others and reads off a p-value. If the training set has examples and the test point’s multiplier comes out as the -th largest, the p-value is

The justification is exchangeability: if the test point really were drawn from the same distribution as the training data, then all multipliers are exchangeable, every ordering is equally likely, and the chance that the test point’s multiplier is the single largest is at most . A small p-value therefore means the tentative label makes the test point look like an outlier, which is strong evidence the label is wrong. The guarantee rests on exchangeability, a weaker assumption than the independent-and-identically-distributed condition usually invoked.

For a binary problem the SVM is fit twice, once per candidate label, giving two p-values. The algorithm predicts the label with the higher p-value (the one under which the test point looks least strange), and then reports confidence and credibility exactly as defined above. For test points at once the same idea applies, but every joint labeling has to be tried, so the SVM is refit times, the cost the paper itself calls impractical past .

Credibility is the part that earns its keep as a reject mechanism. If a prediction’s credibility is low, every label left the test point looking strange, so the safe move is to abstain. The paper notes that the more costly a wrong answer is, the higher the credibility threshold should be set.

Results

The experiments use the US Postal Service database of handwritten digits with a degree-3 polynomial kernel, comparing the new p-value transduction against Vapnik’s margin transduction and a plain SVM. The findings:

  • Credibility flags the errors it should (Table 1). On a task separating ‘8’ from the other digits, the transductive algorithm and a standard SVM misclassified the same three test examples. For all three, credibility came in at 5% or below (4.6%, 4.5%, 0.8%), even though confidence was 95-99%. The low credibility correctly says the data did not support those predictions, while confidence alone would have looked reassuring.

  • Adding the two measures costs nothing in accuracy (Table 2). On a 2-versus-7 task over 20,000 runs at training sizes , the p-value transduction’s error counts track the margin transduction and the standard SVM closely (for example, 262 errors at versus 272 for the SVM, and 186 at versus 191). At the smallest training size it is somewhat worse (640 versus ~522), but the gap closes as grows.

What came after

The scheme is transductive: to score one test point it refits the SVM under every candidate label, and times for joint test points. The strangeness signal is tied to the SVM as well. The work that followed loosened both.

  • The general form. Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer’s Algorithmic Learning in a Random World [2] consolidated the theory so that any nonconformity score, not just an SVM multiplier, drives the calibration.
  • Split conformal prediction. Papadopoulos et al. [3] replaced the per-label retraining with a single held-out calibration set, cheap enough to wrap around any pre-trained model. This is the form most practitioners use today.
  • The deep-learning revival. Angelopoulos and Bates’ tutorial [4] repackaged conformal prediction for modern neural networks and drove the recent wave of distribution-free uncertainty work, including the conformal factuality and conformal language modeling methods built for language models.

My Notes

  • The ICML paper embeds this construction in theory. This paper presents the SVM-rank-of-multipliers method as a standalone practical scheme: take the ranks of SVM Lagrange multipliers, read p-values off them, report confidence and credibility. The companion ICML 1999 paper [5] by the same three authors keeps the construction unchanged but adds a broader theoretical layer: it casts the multipliers as a computable approximation to non-computable measures of algorithmic randomness, and adds a set of impossibility results that bound what conformal-style validity can deliver under iid alone.
  • Modern conformal prediction dropped the abstention signal. Today’s work reports a prediction set at a fixed coverage level, not the per-prediction credibility number that flagged strange inputs. Selective-prediction research keeps rediscovering it as a test on conformal p-values.
  • The reject rule lacks a threshold procedure. Credibility gives a clean basis for abstention, refusing to predict when no label fits, but the paper sets the cutoff only by appeal to how costly a wrong answer would be, with no procedure for choosing it. Split conformal later inverted the problem: fix the error level first and let the calibration set determine the prediction, rather than fixing a strangeness threshold and seeing what error rate follows.

References

  1. Saunders, C., Gammerman, A., and Vovk, V. “Transduction with Confidence and Credibility.” Proceedings of the Sixteenth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 1999), pp. 722–726. https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/99-2/Papers/010.pdf
  2. Vovk, V., Gammerman, A., and Shafer, G. Algorithmic Learning in a Random World. New York: Springer, 2005.
  3. Papadopoulos, H., Proedrou, K., Vovk, V., and Gammerman, A. “Inductive Confidence Machines for Regression.” European Conference on Machine Learning (ECML 2002), pp. 345–356.
  4. Angelopoulos, A. N. and Bates, S. “A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification.” arXiv:2107.07511, 2021. https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07511
  5. Vovk, V., Gammerman, A., and Saunders, C. “Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness.” Proceedings of the Sixteenth International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 1999), pp. 444–453.
  6. Gammerman, A., Vapnik, V., and Vovk, V. “Learning by Transduction.” Proceedings of the Fourteenth Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 1998), pp. 148–156.

item.title: The Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics is a community statement, released today and endorsed by the International Mathematical Union (IMU), that asks mathematicians, professional organizations, governments, and AI companies to set guardrails around AI in mathematical research. It grew out of a September 2025 Lorentz Center conference in Leiden and was drafted over eight months by a 16-person working group convened by Jim Portegies (Eindhoven University of Technology). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20302944.

The declaration is built around recommendations to four audiences: individual mathematicians, mathematical organizations and non-profit funders, policymakers, and commercial AI developers. Those recommendations are preceded by a preamble, a list of values the declaration wants to preserve, and a list of threats it sees from current AI. The pieces:

  • Values it wants to preserve. Proof as the basis of mathematical certainty; results attributable to specific human authors who take responsibility for correctness; transparency and independent verifiability with no proprietary equipment required; shared standards of depth, difficulty, and significance; autonomous community direction-setting on which questions to pursue.
  • Threats it names. Plausible-but-incorrect AI-generated proofs putting peer review under pressure; broken attribution from training data scraped without consent; commercial incentives that distort hiring, funding, and recognition; results announced via press release or blog post before community evaluation; loss of mathematical autonomy as tech-company funding shifts which problems get worked on.
  • For individual mathematicians.
    • Disclose tool use: include a “Tool and computational resource disclosure” section in papers, and as a reviewer follow publisher AI guidelines.
    • Support the needs of reviewing: make peer review easier through disclosure, precise references, and formal proofs where feasible.
    • Adhere to principles of open science: as math research relies more on data and software, follow open-science transparency norms.
    • Retain responsibility for correctness: human authors stay solely responsible for arguments, results, and citations even when AI is used.
    • Affirm the humanity of authorship: credit and responsibility belong to humans, not to automated systems.
    • Put effort into proper attribution: proactively credit human sources, and state explicitly when satisfactory attribution is impossible.
    • Participate in public discourse: support science journalism and contextualize AI-assisted results, especially within your own subfield.
    • Stay informed about emerging tools: track computer-aided math capabilities so you can engage in governance and public discourse.
    • Welcome new contributors: engage researchers crossing into math from other disciplines, and make standards and practices explicit.
    • Consider which tools to use: prefer non-proprietary, energy-efficient, or small-scale systems, and accept delay over violating the declaration’s values.
    • Evaluate ethical consequences: assess downstream uses of your work, withdraw from harmful work, and only enter partnerships consistent with the declaration.
  • For mathematical organizations and non-profit funders.
    • Build expertise and plan strategically: keep abreast of developments, coordinate with publishers and government, and prepare to act on results claimed by unconventional means.
    • Take the lead on publishing and reviewing policies: develop guidelines on disclosure, attribution, authorship, and codes of conduct.
    • Maintain standards of rigor: require human descriptions of central arguments, formal verification, cross-checking, or external pre-submission review.
    • Protect the rights of authors: develop sample licensing agreements, require consent for training-data use, and let authors opt out.
    • Insist on peer-reviewed venues: press releases and blog posts cannot replace journals, proceedings, and books.
    • Support public research laboratories: fund university, national, or international labs studying automated math, independent from industry.
    • Provide frameworks for collaboration: give researchers in industry collaborations access to legal representation and codes of practice.
    • Align funding with values: weigh alignment with the declaration when evaluating and funding academia–industry projects.
  • For policymakers in government and elsewhere.
    • Protect the rights of authors: strengthen legal protections in line with the declaration.
    • Don’t believe the hype: consult mathematicians and other experts rather than press releases or popular reporting on AI capability claims.
    • Regulate the AI industry: increase public oversight, including over military, mass-surveillance, misinformation, and environmental harms.
    • Invest in public computational infrastructure: fund public alternatives to proprietary clouds at university, national, and international levels.
  • For commercial AI.
    • Abide by mathematicians’ standards: any collaboration with mathematicians should meet the disclosure, attribution, correctness, and ethical standards the declaration sets for individuals.
    • Respect freedom of conscience: allow employees and contributors to speak openly about corporate policies and priorities.

Featured endorsements include Peter Scholze (Director, Max Planck Institute for Mathematics), Robbert Dijkgraaf, Kevin Buzzard (Imperial College London), Jeremy Avigad, Leslie Ann Goldberg, and Steven Strogatz. Terence Tao also endorsed the declaration in a Mastodon thread earlier today:

The long-awaited “Leiden Declaration” on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics is now live and seeking signatories: https://leidendeclaration.ai/

This declaration stemmed from a workshop in Leiden University last September on “Mechanization and Mathematical Research”, where it became clear how important it was in the age of AI to make explicit the goals and values of the mathematical community. Many of these goals have long been left implicit, being disseminated informally from advisor to student, or through mechanisms such as the peer review process. So long as the community was largely driven by internal decisions, this implicit system sufficed, and we only needed to share a few explicit goals with the broader public, such as working on unsolved problems, discovering new mathematical phenomena, or applying mathematics to the sciences or other real-world situations.

But in an era where increasingly powerful AI can be set to optimize (or over-optimize) many of the goals that are explicitly presented to them, such an informal state of affairs becomes inadequate, and so the Leiden working group gathered extensive input from the mathematical community to find consensus on what we truly value in mathematics, and how we recommend individual mathematicians, mathematical institutions and external organizations to act. I myself contributed some feedback to an early version of the declaration, but was not part of the working group.

I am very impressed by the final product, which has been refined extensively over the last few months, and endorse it wholeheartedly. Many of the points made in the declaration have also been made elsewhere – my own writings and talks often touch on some subset of these, for instance – but having them all assembled coherently in one document adds significant additional value. I urge everyone in the field to read the declaration, and consider signing it (I myself have already signed).

All the recommendations in the declaration are excellent, but I will highlight “Participate in public discourse”. Perhaps notoriously, practicing mathematicians have a tendency to focus more on technical mathematical tasks, such as solving open problems, than on communicating the purposes of such technical work to the broader public. So long as we had a near-monopoly on the ability to accomplish these tasks, we could have this luxury of only discussing “safe” technical topics in public; but in the new era of “proof abundance”, it is increasingly important that we also debate the “soft” aspects of our field, such as our goals and values.

See also the previous announcement https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24914 by Commelin et al. of the Leiden declaration from March of this year.

EDIT: See also the New York Times article https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/02/science/ai-mathematics-leiden-declaration.html

Related Posts

  • Magnifica Humanitas: Pope Leo XIV’s Encyclical on AI: the sibling institutional response from a different register, where the encyclical takes the broad human-dignity frame and the declaration takes the discipline-specific one. Neither treats AI as neutral.
  • Math Is AGI: Carina Hong on Axiom and Formal Reasoning: the commercial pitch that treats formal mathematical libraries as the training pipeline to AGI, which is the practice the declaration’s commercial-AI section asks for opt-out from.
  • Even Experts Are Surprised by AI’s Latest ‘Vibe-Mathing’ Advance: a concrete recent instance of the press-release-before-peer-review pattern the “Don’t believe the hype” recommendation speaks to.
  • Proof Generation vs Digestion: Tao’s three-part decomposition. His digestion-gap worry and the declaration’s autonomy claim are two views of the same pressure, namely what humans still own once AI generates and verifies most proofs.
  • Terence Tao’s ChatGPT Research Buddy: context for Tao’s coalition role, an active AI user who still signed the declaration and singled out “Participate in public discourse.”
  • LLMs, Copyrighted Training Data, and Fair Use: earlier survey of the consent and copyright question for AI training data, which the declaration’s opt-out clause turns into a specific community-level ask to publishers.

It’s my comeback month! I regained enough strength mid-month and started ramping up. The last 3 weeks’ mileage: 48, 55, 60. I also ran 2 half marathons, and marked my 100th parkrun and 80th HM this month! VO2max recovered from 45.3 to 48.7 in two weeks (all-time high was 54).
